name: Square and Cube Root Basics
description: See square and cube roots as reverse operations, then use product, quotient, fraction and decimal root rules mentally.
script_scope: Teach square root as the number whose square gives the radicand and cube root as the number whose cube gives it. Start with small perfect squares and cubes and make checking by squaring or cubing part of the habit. Teach the chapter laws √(xy)=√x·√y and √(x/y)=√x/√y through friendly products and quotients, then use them on exact fractions and terminating decimals such as 0.0009. Include inside-out evaluation of a short nested-root expression and a capstone that combines product and quotient rules in one radical. Keep all roots exact and positive as used in the chapter. Do not teach prime-factor extraction, long division, surd rationalisation or perfect-square repair here.

name: Square Roots by Prime Factorisation
description: Break a number into prime factors, pair equal factors, and take one factor from each pair to get an exact square root.
script_scope: Teach the factorisation method used in the chapter: resolve a number into primes, group equal prime factors in pairs, and take one factor from each pair. Explain why a perfect square has an even count of every prime factor. Build from small roots to larger integers, then fractions and terminating decimals written as fractions. Include exponent-form shortcuts and recognition of an unpaired factor that prevents an integer square root. Learners should check by squaring the extracted root. Do not yet repair an imperfect square by multiplying or dividing; that belongs to the perfect-square subtopic.

name: Square Roots by Long Division and Approximation
description: Read digits in pairs and build a square root one digit at a time, including decimal and approximate roots.
script_scope: Teach the chapter long-division square-root method without relying on paper-only instructions. Read digits in two-digit periods from the units side; choose the largest first square; carry the remainder into the next period; double the root found so far and choose the next digit that fits. Include a case with a zero inside the root, a three-digit exact root, decimal periods such as 1.5625, tiny decimals such as 0.000441, and a non-perfect root rounded to three decimal places. Teach the chapter fact that the number of root digits equals the number of periods for a perfect square. End with an exact decimal capstone. Every approximation must be labelled as approximate.

name: Perfect Squares and Nearest-Square Problems
description: Recognise square structure and make the smallest possible change that turns a number into a perfect square.
script_scope: Teach perfect-square recognition from even prime exponents and the chapter’s unit-digit clues, including that a square cannot end in 8 and that squares ending in 1 come from unit digits 1 or 9. Cover counting perfect squares in an interval, the greatest and least n-digit perfect squares, least multipliers and divisors that repair odd prime exponents, the least perfect square divisible by several given numbers by starting from their LCM, and least additions or subtractions to reach the nearest square. Include the same reasoning for a small decimal perfect-square adjustment. Make minimality explicit: identify the neighbouring square first, then take the gap.

name: Simplifying Surds and Radical Expressions
description: Pull square factors out of radicals, combine like surds, and spot radical expressions that collapse by identity.
script_scope: Teach surd simplification through hidden perfect-square factors: √(ab)=√a√b, then combine only like surds after simplification. Cover coefficients, addition and subtraction of like surds, products and quotients under roots, conjugate products that become a difference of squares, and expressions built from a supplied approximation such as √2 or √3. Teach recognition of a radical that is itself a perfect square, for example a form matching (√a+√b)^2. End with the chapter-style three-surd square pattern behind √(a+b+c+2√ab+2√bc+2√ca). Explicitly warn that √(a+b) is not generally √a+√b.

name: Rationalisation and Conjugate Radical Forms
description: Remove irrational denominators with a matching conjugate and use conjugate pairs to make difficult surd expressions collapse.
script_scope: Teach rationalisation from the reason it works: conjugates multiply to a difference of squares. Begin with 1/√a, then denominators such as 2+√2 and √5−√3, followed by ratios such as (√5+√3)/(√5−√3). Cover reciprocal conjugate pairs, denominators whose conjugate product is 1, and the chapter pattern where two conjugate-defined quantities make x+y, x²+y² or a reciprocal expression simple. End with a short multi-term rationalisation capstone in the same style as the objective questions. Learners should choose the conjugate from the exact denominator and check that the new denominator is rational.

name: Root Equations and Missing Values
description: Isolate a root or missing radicand, undo the square root by squaring, and check the value in the original equation.
script_scope: Teach the equation patterns used throughout the chapter: √x=k; √(A/x)=k; √(A+x²)=d; a missing radicand inside ordinary arithmetic; and decimal products under a root. Build the habit of isolating the radical before squaring and substituting the answer back. Include the solved-example pattern √86.49+√(5+x²)=12.3, a scale relation where a root of a quotient is known, and a capstone that combines a root equation with ordinary BODMAS. Keep equations at the elementary level used in the chapter and use the positive square root unless the source question explicitly asks otherwise.

name: Infinite Radicals and Telescoping Root Patterns
description: Turn a repeating radical into an equation and make long root sums collapse by rationalising neighbouring terms.
script_scope: Teach self-similar infinite radicals such as √(1+√(1+…)), √(2+√(2+…)) and √(6+√(6+…)): call the whole value x, replace the repeated tail by x, square, solve the quadratic, and keep the positive value. Then teach the telescoping identity 1/(√(n+1)+√n)=√(n+1)−√n and use it to show why middle terms cancel in the chapter’s long sums. Include an alternating rationalised pattern and the 1/(1+√2)+…+1/(√120+√121) style capstone. Learners should expose the repeated or cancelling structure rather than attempting long direct arithmetic.

name: Square-Root Applications and Square Arrangements
description: Translate rows, collections, payments and age-year stories into square or square-root equations.
script_scope: Teach the chapter application patterns where a story hides n² or √n. Cover square arrangements with rows equal to items per row, leftovers after forming the largest square, restoring a damaged square arrangement, distributions where each person receives a multiple of the group size, and collections where each member contributes as many paise as there are members. Include the camel/herd equation containing √x, the nineteenth-century age pattern where a person is x years old in year x², and the payment-per-run pattern where total payment becomes a perfect square. Every story should identify what the unknown represents before forming the equation and should finish with a story-level check.

name: Cube Roots and Perfect Cubes
description: Group prime factors in threes to extract cube roots and repair numbers so every prime exponent is a multiple of three.
script_scope: Teach cube-root extraction by prime factorisation exactly as in the chapter: factor the number, group equal primes in threes, and take one from each triple. Extend to large exact cubes, fractions and terminating decimals. Teach that perfect-cube prime exponents are multiples of three, then find least multipliers and divisors, the greatest four-digit perfect cube, and the least addition needed to reach the next cube. End with the chapter rationalising-factor pattern for ∛9−∛3+1, using a=∛3 so a²−a+1 multiplied by a+1 becomes a³+1. Check cube-root answers by cubing them.
